title: CFA Ethics 37: When an algorithm decides - who is responsible
subtitle: Reasonable basis for a model, bias in the data, and the duty to explain it to clients
whyItMatters: The standards were written for humans making decisions, and they apply unchanged when a model decides instead - but how they apply has to be rethought. This is the fastest-growing part of the curriculum.
openingQuestion: A machine learning model produces an investment recommendation whose internal workings you cannot explain. How does Standard V(A) apply?
openingOptions: It does not, since the model made the decision rather than you
It applies unchanged: understand the data, assumptions and limits
Only if the model was built by your own firm's own team
It applies more lightly, since a model is more objective
explanation: Standard V(A) requires a reasonable basis for every recommendation, and a recommendation coming from a model creates no exception. What changes is the content of "understanding it well enough": for a model that means knowing where the training data came from and what bias it carries, knowing what objective the model was optimised for, knowing the conditions in which it performs poorly, and having a way to detect when it starts drifting away from the conditions it learned. Not being able to explain each internal weight is acceptable; not knowing where the model will break is not.

summary.keyIdea: Standard V(A) applies unchanged to a recommendation from a model - responsibility for the reasonable basis belongs to whoever issues the recommendation and cannot be transferred to an algorithm.
summary.commonMistake: Treating the model as an objective third party. It is a tool whose data and training a person chose, so every bias in it is the user's bias.

application.title: What must be explainable
application.message: Why the model produced this recommendation. Not being able to explain it means there is no reasonable basis in the sense V(A) intends.

sections.text: When an investment recommendation comes from a model, the first question is who is responsible. The standards' answer is short: still whoever signs the recommendation.
The requirement for a reasonable basis has no exception for machine-generated recommendations. What changes is the content of understanding it well enough.

sections.label: What understanding a model well enough means
sections.text: Knowing where the training data came from and what bias it carries. Knowing what objective the model was optimised for. Knowing the conditions in which it performs poorly. And having a way to detect when the market has drifted away from the conditions it learned.

Not being able to explain each internal weight is acceptable - most modern models are like that. Not knowing where the model will break is not, because at that point you have no basis for saying whether this recommendation is still trustworthy.
A risk particular to machine output

A figure produced by a model looks more objective than a person's opinion, so users question it less. That effect raises the risk rather than lowering it. Standard V(B) therefore comes into play too: clients must know a model is involved in the decision and know its limits.
The boundary of understanding it well enough

left.label: Sufficient reasonable basis
left.text: You cannot explain why the model put a weight of 0.31 on a variable - and you do not need to. But you know it was trained on 2010-2020 data, a period with no significant interest rate shock; you know it optimises for 12-month return rather than for maximum drawdown; and you know it degrades badly when liquidity is thin. You can say where it will break.

right.label: Insufficient reasonable basis
right.text: The model has a good backtest record and you use its output, but you do not know what period the training data covers, what objective it optimises for, or what conditions make it wrong. A past record does not substitute for understanding the model - and that is precisely where Standard V(A) grants machines no exception.

sections.label: A number looks more objective than an opinion, and that is a risk rather than a reassurance
sections.text: A recommendation written in prose invites challenge: the reader sees at once that it is one person's view. The same recommendation presented as a score of 7.4/10 is rarely questioned, even though it rests on the same assumptions. The consequence for the duty to explain: you must state that this is a model's output and what the model rests on, rather than letting the number manufacture a certainty it does not have.

lines: So responsibility stays exactly where it was.

diagram.label: V(A) applies unchanged to a recommendation from a model
Understanding enough: the data, the objective, the breaking conditions
Bias in the training data becomes bias in the recommendation
V(B): clients must know a model is involved in the decision

realWorldExample.company: Data bias does not vanish because the model is a machine
realWorldExample.description: A model trained on data from a rising market learns that risk is always rewarded, and it will keep believing that until it meets a different period. What is dangerous is that the model states that conclusion with the confidence of an arithmetic result rather than the hesitancy of a judgment. This is why Standard V(A) applies to models more strictly rather than less: output that looks objective is questioned less.

quiz.question: How does Standard V(A) apply to a recommendation from a model?
options: It does not apply at all, since a human did not make the decision
Unchanged - whoever issues it still needs a reasonable basis
More lightly, since a model is more objective than a person
Only if the model was built in-house by the firm itself
quiz.explanation: The tool changes, the duty does not; what changes is the specific content of understanding it well enough. Ownership of the model is beside the point - a bought model needs the same scrutiny as a built one, and arguably more, since you did not watch it being made. And treating machine output as more objective inverts the risk: a number that looks impartial gets challenged less, so the duty to check it is heavier rather than lighter.

quiz.question: What does "understanding the model well enough" mean here?
options: Being able to rebuild that model from scratch with your own tools
Being able to explain every weight and parameter inside the model
Knowing the data, the optimisation objective, and where it breaks
Holding a professional qualification in machine learning and data science
quiz.explanation: Not being able to explain each internal weight is acceptable - most modern models are opaque in exactly that way. Not knowing where the model will break is not, because without that you cannot say whether today's output is still trustworthy. Rebuilding it yourself and holding a data science qualification are both far more than the standard asks, and neither would tell you what the training data actually covered.

quiz.question: Why is bias in the training data particularly dangerous?
options: Because regulators prohibit using historical data for training
Because training data is always deleted once the model is finished
Because bias makes the model run more slowly than it needs to
Because the model states its conclusion with the confidence of arithmetic
quiz.explanation: Output that looks objective is questioned less, so the same distortion does more damage when it arrives from a machine than when a person says it out loud. Historical data is the only kind there is for training, so no rule forbids it; the data is normally retained precisely so the bias can be examined later; and speed has nothing to do with it. The danger is confidence, not performance.

quiz.question: What does Standard V(B) require when a model takes part in an investment decision?
options: Clients must know the model is involved and know its limits
The model's source code must be provided to clients for review
Clients must choose between the model and human judgment
Nothing further, since the process is an internal matter
quiz.explanation: This is V(B)'s 'describe the process' element: the client chose you on the basis of a particular process, so a change in that process has to be communicated. That does not extend to handing over source code, which would tell most clients nothing and is proprietary besides. Nor does the client get a vote on methodology - they get the information needed to judge it, which is not the same thing.

quiz.question: What does model drift mean in the context of Standard V(A)?
options: The model runs progressively slower as the data volume grows
The relationship it learned drifts from reality, with no error raised
The model hits a technical fault and stops returning any results at all
Users gradually stop believing in the model's results
quiz.explanation: The danger is that nothing raises an error: the model keeps returning normal-looking figures while the relationship underneath them has stopped holding. A technical fault would at least be visible, slower performance is an engineering matter rather than an ethical one, and a loss of user confidence is a symptom that arrives long after the drift itself - usually after money has been lost.

keyTakeaways: Standard V(A) applies unchanged to a recommendation from a model
Understanding enough = knowing the data, the objective, and the breaking conditions
Not explaining each weight is fine; not knowing where it breaks is not
Output that looks objective is questioned less - so the risk is higher
V(B): clients must know a model is involved and know its limits

practicePrompt.question: Your firm's asset allocation model has worked well for five years. Results have deteriorated recently but nobody has re-examined it. What is your duty?
options: Wait for more data, since five good years is strong evidence
Review whether the market still matches the training data
Stop using the model and revert to manual judgment
Pass responsibility to the team that built the model
practicePrompt.explanation: Five good years is exactly what makes people wait, and that is the trap - a model that has drifted from the conditions it learned keeps returning normal-looking figures while the basis underneath them has lapsed. Two standards fire at once: V(A) demands a reasonable basis for the recommendation you are issuing today, and V(B) demands telling clients if the investment process has changed.
